excerpts.authority: Egyptian Electric Utility and Consumer Protection Regulatory Agency (EgyptERA)
excerpts.documentTitle: EgyptERA Circular No. 3 of 2023 (self-consumption solar generation)
excerpts.text: A grid-connected self-consumption solar plant must supply the subscriber's internal electrical loads and must include technical protection to prevent generated electricity from being exported to the public electricity grid. The installed capacity of the plant may not exceed the subscriber's maximum electrical load recorded during the preceding financial year, and the maximum self-consumption plant capacity is 30 MW per subscriber. The project must comply with the applicable electricity distribution/transmission code, the solar photovoltaic technical code, and Egyptian equipment and electrical safety standards, and must be implemented by a company qualified by the New and Renewable Energy Authority (NREA). Plants above 10 MW require a separate meter measuring total solar generation at the internal connection point.

excerpts.authority: Egyptian Electric Utility and Consumer Protection Regulatory Agency (EgyptERA)
excerpts.documentTitle: EgyptERA Circular No. 3 of 2023 (self-consumption permit and licence thresholds)
excerpts.text: A self-consumption plant owned and operated by the electricity subscriber may qualify for an exemption from the electricity-generation permit and licence when its capacity does not exceed 500 kW. Where a qualified solar company instead owns the plant and sells electricity to the subscriber under a power-purchase arrangement, that company must apply to EgyptERA for the applicable permit and licence regardless of capacity. Self-consumption projects above 500 kW generally require an EgyptERA construction permit, an electricity-generation licence, a grid-impact or network-impact study at the subscriber's cost, and completion of any network reinforcement identified by the distribution company.

excerpts.authority: Egyptian Electric Utility and Consumer Protection Regulatory Agency (EgyptERA)
excerpts.documentTitle: EgyptERA Circular No. 3 of 2023, as amended by Circular No. 6 of 2023 (site-control requirement)
excerpts.text: Ownership of the installation site (roof or land) is not mandatory. The applicant may instead submit an ownership contract, lease, or documented right-of-use agreement, provided the document covers the installation site for at least 25 years, expressly authorizes installation and operation of the solar plant, identifies the relevant building or area, and permits access for installation, operation, maintenance, and inspection. The 2023 amendment (Circular No. 6 of 2023) also allows the solar plant to be located outside the subscriber's main property under specific conditions, including site control, physical proximity, and a private cable connection that does not use the public distribution or transmission network.

excerpts.authority: Egyptian Electric Utility and Consumer Protection Regulatory Agency (EgyptERA)
excerpts.documentTitle: EgyptERA Circular No. 4 of 2026 (net-metering capacity and local content)
excerpts.section: net-metering capacity band and local content
excerpts.text: The published net-metering procedures cover projects with capacities up to 20 MW, subject to the technical ability of the distribution network to accommodate the project at the proposed connection point; 20 MW is a regulatory scheme ceiling, not a guaranteed right to connect. The circular also establishes a national net-metering capacity target of approximately 1,000 MW AC through 2030, including previously connected capacity. Net-metering projects must satisfy a minimum local-content requirement of approximately 25% of total project components, reviewed through the NREA PV-HUB process.

excerpts.authority: Egyptian Electric Utility and Consumer Protection Regulatory Agency (EgyptERA)
excerpts.documentTitle: EgyptERA Circular No. 4 of 2026 (net-metering process and timelines)
excerpts.text: The published net-metering process runs: NREA local-content review (approximately 15 days); distribution-company confirmation of available network capacity (approximately one week); preparation of the technical file by an NREA-qualified solar company; payment of the study fee; construction within six months for plants up to 500 kW or one year for larger plants; distribution-company testing (approximately three weeks); and bidirectional meter installation and energization (approximately three weeks after successful testing and payment). Regulatory charges are EGP 4,000 for technical-file and measurement review up to 500 kW (EGP 3,000 for repeat measurements), and EGP 30,000 above 500 kW (EGP 5,000 for repeat measurements), plus the approved cost of the bidirectional meter.

Constructing buildings or facilities, opening roads, or undertaking industrial or commercial activities inside a declared protected area requires approval from the competent environmental authority. The law may also restrict activities in a designated surrounding or buffer area where they could affect the protected area, its natural resources, or its ecological characteristics. A project located inside or near a protected area should obtain confirmation from the EEAA Nature Conservation Sector on whether a separate protected-area activity permit is required.

excerpts.authority: Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency (EEAA), under Environmental Law No. 4 of 1994
excerpts.documentTitle: Environmental Law No. 4 of 1994 (executive regulations) and EEAA environmental-impact-assessment guidance
excerpts.text: A new industrial solar installation, or an extension or modification of an existing industrial facility, may require environmental review before construction or operation. The self-consumption application checklist expressly requires EEAA-approved environmental clearance for applicable projects; the residential exemption does not apply to an industrial facility. EEAA's environmental-impact-assessment guidance includes compact solar power installations within its indicative Category B project list (typically reviewed within about 30 days), though the final classification (Category A, B, or C) depends on plant capacity, location, and environmental sensitivity.
